Consult Summary:
- 50-year-old woman with 5–6 days of continuous dry cough, rhinorrhea, myalgias and subjective fevers/chills; clinical impression is most consistent with a viral upper respiratory infection/acute bronchitis (DDx also includes influenza, COVID-19, and ACE inhibitor–related cough).

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Persistent, continuous dry cough for ~5–6 days that is worse at night and interrupts sleep; associated runny nose and sore/irritated throat from coughing.
  - Generalized myalgias, marked fatigue/weakness and subjective chills/feeling feverish (no temperature measured).
  - Brief diarrheal episode at onset that resolved after the first day.
- Timeline/progression:
  - Symptoms began approximately 5–6 days prior to visit.
  - Diarrhea lasted briefly at onset and has resolved; cough has persisted without improvement.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Cough worse at night; rest and time suggested as supportive measures. No specific relieving medications reported.
- Associated symptoms/systems review:
  - No measured fever documented.
  - No reported dyspnea at baseline (only transient breathlessness during coughing spells).
  - No chest pain, no ear symptoms, no vomiting, appetite largely preserved.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No hemoptysis, no purulent sputum, no focal chest pain, no ear discharge, no reported loss of taste/smell documented.

Past Medical History:
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus — followed by primary care; reportedly controlled.
- Hypertension — reportedly controlled.

Medications:
- Metformin — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Lisinopril — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Allergies: None reported.

Social History:
- Lives with partner (partner currently asymptomatic).
- Occupation: Software developer (mostly sedentary).
- Tobacco: Former smoker; quit ~6 months ago.
- Alcohol: Drinks wine ~2–3 glasses on ~3 evenings per week.
- No other substance use documented.
- Function: Missed initial sick day, returned to work intermittently but fatigue limits activity.

Family History:
- Father with type 2 diabetes mellitus. No other family history documented.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings: Cough audible during encounter; no other formal physical exam findings documented.

Investigations:
- None ordered or performed during this consult; no imaging or laboratory results documented.

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
- Working diagnosis: Viral upper respiratory infection / acute bronchitis — most consistent with the history of 5–6 days of rhinorrhea, continuous dry nocturnal cough, myalgias, subjective fever/chills and transient diarrhea. Clinician counseling during visit supports viral etiology and symptomatic management.

DDx Integration (brief):
- Viral URI / Acute bronchitis (High likelihood)
  - Supporting: Recent onset (5–6 days) rhinorrhea, dry cough worse at night, myalgias and subjective fever; clinician concluded viral illness.
  - Opposing: No objective temperature recorded; if cough persists beyond expected course, reconsider.
- Influenza (Medium likelihood)
  - Supporting: Prominent myalgias, chills, marked fatigue with acute cough and rhinorrhea.
  - Opposing: No documented high fever or abrupt severe onset; partner asymptomatic.
- ACE inhibitor–induced cough (Lisinopril) (Medium likelihood)
  - Supporting: Patient is taking lisinopril; cough is dry and nocturnal which can be consistent.
  - Opposing: Onset coincided with other systemic viral symptoms (feverishness, myalgias, diarrhea) making infectious cause more likely.

Issue 1: Acute cough / suspected viral upper respiratory infection (acute bronchitis)
- Assessment:
  - Most likely viral URI/acute bronchitis causing dry, persistent cough and systemic viral symptoms.
- Plan:
  - Symptomatic care: rest, maintain hydration.
  - Analgesic/antipyretic: Paracetamol (per clinician advice) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Occupational advice: Consider taking 1–2 days off work to rest; return when feeling better.
  - Safety-netting: Return earlier if breathing worsens, if fever persists or is confirmed, if cough substantially worsens, or if new concerning symptoms develop.
  - Follow-up: Reassess in 2–3 days if not improving; clinician indicated possible consideration of antibiotics if patient remains febrile and cough not improving (decision to be made on re-evaluation).

Issue 2: Consideration of alternative causes if cough persists
- Assessment:
  - If cough persists beyond expected viral course, consider post-viral cough, ACE inhibitor–induced cough, COVID-19, or other causes per DDx.
- Plan:
  - If persistent beyond the next several days or at follow-up, evaluate for alternative etiologies (medication review including lisinopril, consider COVID-19 testing if appropriate locally, and further clinical assessment/exam and investigations such as chest exam, CXR or labs as indicated).
  - Do not empirically stop lisinopril without clinical review (no medication changes documented during this consult).

Issue 3: Chronic conditions — diabetes and hypertension
- Assessment:
  - Both conditions reported as under routine care and controlled.
- Plan:
  - Continue current medications (Metformin and lisinopril) as prescribed; doses not specified in chart.
  - Counseling: Advised consideration of reducing alcohol intake in context of diabetes and hypertension (clinician recommended stepwise reduction).

General plan items:
- Provide symptomatic treatment and self-care advice (rest, fluids, paracetamol).
- Return for earlier review if worsening respiratory symptoms or breathing difficulty.
- Re-evaluate in 2–3 days if no improvement; consider antibiotics only if persistent fever and cough suggest bacterial infection on reassessment.
- Address persistent cough and medication review (ACE inhibitor) if symptoms do not resolve.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: No vital signs recorded; no formal physical exam findings beyond an audible cough; no diagnostic testing or results documented; medication doses/route/frequency not documented.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None identified — DDx considerations (influenza, COVID-19, ACE inhibitor cough) are consistent with the transcript; clinician favored viral cause.
- Transcript quality: Mostly clear; occasional conversational pauses and minor overlapping speech but sufficient for documentation.
